subject: biology

items.q: A single neurone carries impulses from a receptor in the toe to the spinal cord. Which statement best explains how this structure is adapted to its function?
items.correct: It is long, so impulses reach the CNS quickly.
items.misconception: It detects the stimulus and causes the response.
items.why: Detection and response often happen in the same part of the body, such as the hand touching something hot, so students merge the two roles into one structure. Information from receptors passes along cells (neurones) as electrical impulses to the central nervous system. The CNS coordinates the response of effectors, which may be muscles contracting or glands secreting hormones, so receptor and effector are different structures in the pathway stimulus → receptor → coordinator → effector → response.
items.random_wrong: It is part of the central nervous system.

items.q: Effectors in the human body may be:
items.correct: muscles contracting or glands secreting
items.misconception: receptors detecting light and sound levels
items.why: Detection and response often happen in the same part of the body, such as the hand touching something hot, so students merge the two roles into one structure. Information from receptors passes along cells (neurones) as electrical impulses to the central nervous system. The CNS coordinates the response of effectors, which may be muscles contracting or glands secreting hormones, so receptor and effector are different structures in the pathway stimulus → receptor → coordinator → effector → response.
items.random_wrong: skeletal muscles moving bones at a joint

items.q: In a reflex arc, what is the function of the relay neurone?
items.correct: It links the sensory neurone to the motor neurone.
items.misconception: It carries the impulse to the conscious brain.
items.why: The person is usually awake and aware of what happened, and they notice the movement, so they assume they chose it. Reflex actions are automatic and rapid; they do not involve the conscious part of the brain. Awareness of what happened comes after the response, not before it.
items.random_wrong: It carries the electrical impulse across the synapse.

items.q: Why is a reflex action important when a person touches a very hot object?
items.correct: It is automatic and rapid, so injury is reduced.
items.misconception: It gives the person time to decide how to act.
items.why: The person is usually awake and aware of what happened, and they notice the movement, so they assume they chose it. Reflex actions are automatic and rapid; they do not involve the conscious part of the brain. Awareness of what happened comes after the response, not before it.
items.random_wrong: It keeps the impulse out of the nervous system.

items.q: A table shows one student's mean reaction time in three trials: trial 1, 0.28 s; trial 2, 0.24 s; trial 3, 0.21 s. What do these data show?
items.correct: The reaction time fell across the trials.
items.misconception: The reaction time rose across the trials.
items.why: In most measurements a bigger number means 'more' or 'better', so a taller bar on a chart is read as a better performance. Reaction time is the time taken to respond, so the smaller the value the faster the response. On a bar chart or graph of reaction times, a lower bar or point shows the quicker reaction.
items.random_wrong: The student reacted more slowly each time.

items.q: Four students have mean reaction times of 0.15 s, 0.22 s, 0.28 s and 0.31 s. These values are drawn as a bar chart. Which statement about the chart is correct?
items.correct: The tallest bar is the 0.31 s time.
items.misconception: The tallest bar is the fastest time.
items.why: In most measurements a bigger number means 'more' or 'better', so a taller bar on a chart is read as a better performance. Reaction time is the time taken to respond, so the smaller the value the faster the response. On a bar chart or graph of reaction times, a lower bar or point shows the quicker reaction.
items.random_wrong: The shortest bar is the slowest time.

items.q: A patient can no longer coordinate their movements or keep their balance after an injury to the brain. Which is the most likely cause?
items.correct: The cerebellum is damaged
items.misconception: Damage within the medulla
items.why: The cerebellum and medulla are both drawn low down and towards the back of a brain diagram, and both are linked with things we do not think about. The brain has different regions that carry out different functions: the cerebral cortex is responsible for consciousness, intelligence, memory and language; the cerebellum coordinates muscular activity and balance; the medulla controls unconscious activities such as heart rate and breathing rate.

items.q: Neuroscientists want to find out which region of a patient's brain controls speech. Which statement explains why this is difficult?
items.correct: The brain is complex and easily damaged.
items.misconception: Damaged brain regions are simple to repair.
items.why: Detailed scan images look complete, so students assume that seeing a structure means it can be understood and repaired. Neuroscientists have mapped regions of the brain to particular functions by studying patients with brain damage, electrically stimulating different parts of the brain and using MRI scanning techniques, but the complexity and delicacy of the brain makes investigating and treating brain disorders very difficult.
items.random_wrong: MRI scanning shows which cells are working.

items.q: Which statement correctly relates a structure of the eye to its function?
items.correct: The retina contains receptors for light.
items.misconception: The cornea changes shape to focus images.
items.why: The cornea does refract light entering the eye, and students hear that laser surgery changes the shape of the cornea, so they assume the cornea is what adjusts the focus. Accommodation is the process of changing the shape of the lens to focus on near or distant objects. The cornea refracts light entering the eye but does not change shape to focus it.
items.random_wrong: The iris narrows the pupil in dim lighting.

items.q: A person walks out of bright sunlight into a dark room. What happens in the eye?
items.correct: The iris muscles make the pupil wider.
items.misconception: The iris muscles make the pupil narrower.
items.why: Students associate narrowing the eyes with trying to see, and rarely watch a pupil change in a mirror as the light level falls. The eye adapts to dim light by the iris muscles widening the pupil, allowing more light to reach the receptors in the retina. In bright light the iris muscles narrow the pupil to protect the retina.
items.random_wrong: The ciliary muscles make the lens thicker.

items.q: A student looks up from a book and focuses on a tree in the distance. What happens in the eye?
items.correct: The ciliary muscles relax and the lens is pulled thin.
items.misconception: The ciliary muscles contract and the lens thickens.
items.why: Students assume that a contracting muscle must pull the suspensory ligaments tight, when contracting the ring of ciliary muscle actually makes the ring smaller and slackens the ligaments. To focus on a near object the ciliary muscles contract, the suspensory ligaments loosen and the lens is thicker. To focus on a distant object the ciliary muscles relax, the suspensory ligaments are pulled tight and the lens is pulled thin.
items.random_wrong: The suspensory ligaments loosen and the lens bulges.

items.q: A ray diagram shows light from a distant object coming to a focus in front of the retina. Which defect is shown, and how is it corrected?
items.correct: Myopia, corrected with a concave lens.
items.misconception: Myopia, corrected with a convex lens.
items.why: The names 'short' and 'long' sightedness are read as describing where the light lands rather than the distance at which the person can see clearly, so the two defects are swapped. In myopia rays of light focus in front of the retina and a concave spectacle lens spreads the rays out so that they focus on the retina. In hyperopia rays focus behind the retina and a convex spectacle lens refracts them more strongly so that they focus on the retina.
items.random_wrong: Hyperopia, corrected with a convex lens.

items.q: A person is exercising hard and their body temperature rises above normal. What happens in the skin?
items.correct: Blood vessels dilate and sweat is produced.
items.misconception: Blood vessels move nearer the skin surface.
items.why: Textbook diagrams of hot and cold skin are often drawn with the vessels at different depths, which looks like movement rather than a change in width. If the body temperature is too high, blood vessels dilate (vasodilation) and sweat is produced from the sweat glands. Both these mechanisms cause a transfer of energy from the skin to the environment. The vessels change width; they do not change position.
items.random_wrong: Blood vessels constrict and shivering starts.

items.q: A person waits at a bus stop in cold weather and their body temperature begins to fall. How does the body raise it again?
items.correct: Blood vessels constrict and shivering starts.
items.misconception: Blood vessels dilate and shivering begins.
items.why: Textbook diagrams of hot and cold skin are often drawn with the vessels at different depths, which looks like movement rather than a change in width. If the body temperature is too high, blood vessels dilate (vasodilation) and sweat is produced from the sweat glands. Both these mechanisms cause a transfer of energy from the skin to the environment. The vessels change width; they do not change position.
items.random_wrong: Narrowing blood vessels cause the shivering.

items.q: Which parts of the nervous system make up the central nervous system?
items.correct: The brain and the spinal cord only.
items.misconception: The central nervous system includes all the nerves in the body, including those in the arms and legs.
items.why: The words 'nervous system' and 'central nervous system' are used loosely in everyday speech, and diagrams often show the brain, spinal cord and nerves in one colour. The CNS is the brain and spinal cord. Neurones carrying impulses from receptors to the CNS, and from the CNS to effectors, are not part of the CNS.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How does information pass from one neurone to the next at a synapse?
items.correct: A chemical is released and diffuses across the gap, setting off a new electrical impulse in the next neurone.
items.misconception: The electrical impulse passes straight across the synapse from one neurone into the next.
items.why: Students learn that impulses are electrical and picture the reflex arc as one continuous wire, so the gap at the synapse is overlooked. Impulses travel along neurones as electrical impulses, but at a synapse a chemical diffuses across the gap and starts a new electrical impulse in the next neurone.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the impulse in a reflex arc pass through the central nervous system?
items.correct: Yes. The impulse passes through a relay neurone in the CNS, even though the conscious part of the brain is not involved.
items.misconception: Because a reflex is not conscious, the impulse does not pass through the central nervous system at all.
items.why: Students equate the CNS with conscious thought, so 'not conscious' is read as 'not in the brain or spinal cord'. In a reflex arc the sensory neurone passes the impulse across a synapse to a relay neurone in the CNS, which passes it on to the motor neurone. The CNS still coordinates the response; only the conscious part of the brain is not involved.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which part of the body monitors and controls body temperature?
items.correct: The thermoregulatory centre in the brain monitors and controls body temperature.
items.misconception: The skin monitors and controls body temperature by itself, without the brain being involved.
items.why: Sweating, shivering and changes in skin colour all happen in the skin, so students treat the skin as the control centre rather than as the place where the response happens. Body temperature is monitored and controlled by the thermoregulatory centre in the brain, which contains receptors sensitive to the temperature of the blood. The skin contains temperature receptors and sends nervous impulses to the thermoregulatory centre.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can a gland be an effector?
items.correct: Yes. Effectors may be muscles contracting or glands secreting hormones.
items.misconception: Only muscles can act as effectors.
items.why: The examples used most often, such as pulling a hand away or shivering, all involve movement, so glands are forgotten. The CNS coordinates the response of effectors which may be muscles contracting or glands secreting hormones, so a gland secreting a hormone is just as much an effector as a contracting muscle.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What causes shivering when body temperature is too low?
items.correct: Skeletal muscles contract rapidly (shiver) in response to impulses from the thermoregulatory centre.
items.misconception: Shivering is caused by the blood vessels in the skin narrowing.
items.why: The words 'constrict' and 'contract' sound alike, and both responses to cold are learned together, so students link them as cause and effect. If the body temperature is too low, blood vessels constrict (vasoconstriction), sweating stops and skeletal muscles contract (shiver). These are separate responses coordinated by the thermoregulatory centre; vasoconstriction does not cause shivering.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: One student's reaction time improves over three trials. What can be concluded from this?
items.correct: That this student's reaction time improved over these three trials.
items.misconception: A pattern in one person's results shows what would happen for other people too.
items.why: Students are used to drawing a single conclusion from a practical, and a clear trend in a small table looks convincing on its own. Data extracted from a graph, chart or table describe the individuals actually measured. A conclusion about the functioning of the nervous system in other people needs data from those people as well.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
